Bulungula Attacks

By: Catherine Rice | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Eastern Cape's picturesque Wild Coast has been hit by a wave of violent crimes that is threatening its tourism market.

Unique Selling Point:
In the most recent attack, in August, Wild Coast community developers Dave Martin and his wife Rejane Woodroffe were violently attacked in their home, beaten up and kidnapped. They survived the ordeal, but say criminals from outside the area have been infiltrating the once peaceful villages, and communities are now living in fear of who will be next.

Summary:
Dave Martin and his wife Rejane Woodroffe are founders of the Bulungula Incubator NGO and Bulungula Lodge and have lived in the area for twenty years. They were pistol-whipped and beaten with beer bottles during the August attack at Nqileni village in Xhorha Mouth. They were also kidnapped - the four gun-wielding attackers took them in their vehicle, but later released them and fled on foot. In April, a family that runs a creche in the area was also violently attacked. In February, Bulungula Education programme manager Lindiwe Tukane was attacked by two gunmen who stole her car and laptop.

Further information:
The wave of violent incidents started in November, less than a year ago, with the murder of a trading store owner Peter Venter. He was killed in what's believed to have been a botched armed robbery. Community members believe criminals see the remote rural villages as easy targets. The closest police station to the Bulungula Lodge is two hours away. Dave Martin and his wife Rejane are committed to continuing their upliftment work. They have created 180 permanent jobs, and remain dedicated to addressing "systemic injustices that contribute to criminal behaviour".

Script:


UPSOUND He kicked her in her face and I said ay rather you shoot me. He said no I’ve got a bullet for you.

UPSOUND My son they tied him very very tight it was very painful.

UPSOUND One of them just came in and went straight for me and hit me on head and I just went down. And that was the start of the whole story.

VO 1 The Eastern Cape’s Wild Coast, a place as remote as it is beautiful.

VO 2 For the past twenty years, Dave Martin and his wife Rejane Woodroffe have called it home.

VO 3 In the Nqileni Village, about 60kms from the nearest town Elliotdale, they built a tourist lodge called Bulungula - now 100% community-owned. And helped raise funds for important social projects like pre-schools, water tanks and healthcare.

UPSOUND Dave Martin: The community provided the land and I had been working in the UK and managed to save some pounds and used that money to build the rondavels.

VO 4 At first, Rejane commuted between Cape Town, where she worked as an economist, and the Wild Coast. By 2008, she had quit her job and moved here permanently.

VO 5 Like much of the Wild Coast, the money generated by tourism is vital to Nqileni. The lodge was a godsend and an ideal fit for this close-knit community.

UPSOUND Rejane Woodroffe: When I came to this community, it was just astounding to be part of the way human beings were meant to live. Which is in cohesive communities which have this long history. Of living together. An ancient way of life that is continuous.

VO 6 But, that history of cohesiveness - where an injury to one is an injury to all - is at risk. The spectre of violent crime is casting a dark shadow across this remote rural landscape, threatening not only the lives of the people who live here but their economic survival too.

PAUSE

VO 7 Less than a year ago, the owner of this trading store was brutally murdered. Employing 75 staff, Peter Venter was killed in what’s believed to have been a botched armed robbery. A hive of activity for 24 years, it’s now eerily quiet.

VO 8 With the suspects still on the loose, the incident marked the beginning of a wave of violent attacks in the area - each month bringing a new victim.

UPSOUND Dave Martin: We realised then that this was unprecedented. These kinds of things just don’t happen in our rural villages you know. So we took a lot of measures then to make sure our community was protected. We created access control to make sure vehicles couldn’t just drive in, put up cameras, put up panic alarms in huts. We thought we were safe.

VO 9 But they weren’t. Last month, as Dave arrived home, he and Rejane would become the latest victims in this series of attacks.

UPSOUND Dave Martin: Suddenly, I see four men running at me. I ran off and fell down a small cliff, and that’s when I got injured in that process. They tied me up, beat me and brought me into our hut.

UPSOUND Rejane Woodroffe: I just remember thinking Ok I guess its happening to us now. And then I got hit over the head with a gun.

VO 10 Dave pressed his panic button, and a neighbour called - but with a gun to his head, he was forced to say it had been a false alarm.

NATSOUND Re enactment (Dave speaking in Xhosa) “Sorry Tata it was a mistake. There’s no problem. Thank you”.

UPSOUND Rejane Woodroffe: They were looking for a safe, they were looking for, they said R500 000 which of course we don’t have. But even if it was copycats or whatever right they got so much money from the trading store so they think there’s another white guy down there so he must have money too. But, they pretty much got a thousand rand cash. But now they become agitated because when they don’t get what they want they can hurt us cos they start threatening us again. Walk to offices..

VO 11 Part of their ordeal was caught on camera.

UPSOUND Dave Martin: We went into the offices and they did some more ransacking looking for laptops and things like that.

VO 12 Dashcam footage showed the couple being kidnapped in the car owned by their non-profit organisation.

NATSOUND Dashcam footage of them laughing

UPSOUND Dave Martin: The security guard, he luckily in that time ran off and warned everyone in the community.
UPSOUND Rejane Martin: Dave’s lung had collapsed at that point, so he was in a bad way. All the whatsapp groups started and this is half past nine, ten at night, people were barricading the road to stop the car and then the lights of the different cars that had been alerted, and then they started plans to abandon the car. They jumped out of car and ran, and slashed three of the tyres, but I managed to turn around the car and drive. And then there were lots of people everywhere.

VO 13 The community has rallied around Dave and Rejane since the attack.

UPSOUND Nkosi Zwelikhanyile / Traditional leader: I want to thank you children of God for supporting my brother Dave. He arrived here and was welcomed by my mother as a child of my home. We gave him the man’s name the one who tries to fix things.

VO 14 Traditional leader Nkosi Zwelikhanyile addressed the community on the way forward - young men will do nightly patrols. The community will stand together.

UPSOUND Nkosi Zwelikhanyile: The tsotsis are fewer than us. We are many. We cannot be defeated by the tsotsis”.

UPSOUND Dave Martin: This is not something that affects me alone. It affects all of us. It’s going to change the way we live.

LINK: Rejane and Dave have created 180 permanent jobs on the Wild Coast as a result of their community development work. Despite enduring such a brutal attack, they remain committed to staying in the area. In fact, their passion for community upliftment remains stronger than ever.

VO 15 But, they’re frustrated by the lack of police action - and believe the men who attacked them are the same criminals responsible for other attacks in the area.

VO 16 One of them was Lindiwe Tukane. A resident here for the past 12 years, she was one of this crime wave’s first victims…attacked in February this year.

UPSOUND Lindiwe Tukane: They tied me. Like this, just here only. They went through everything, like they opened all my suitcases and when they opened like this throw things down.

VO 17 Lindiwe remembered fearing her neighbours would be next. Like her, many worked for the Bulungula Incubator, the non profit organisation co founded by Dave and Rejane.

UPSOUND Lindiwe Tukane: They said Wena you are the one who is going to wake up those white people next door. I thought anything that could happen to them I won’t live with myself. I said I don’t know them let’s not even go there.

VO 18 Lindiwe and her son were left in a forest five kms away - gagged and tied up. Her car hasn’t been recovered.

MASA: How do you feel that they haven’t been arrested yet?

UPSOUND Lindiwe Tukane: Besides fearing them that they will come back, I am angry.

UPSOUND Dave Martin: We’ve got photos of these guys, names of them and no one’s been arrested.I would hope they would be consolidated into this is a gang operating in an area, and the consequences of what they’re doing is not just their crimes, its the destruction of a way of life for traditional communities in a remote area.

LINK: We’ve been in contact with the police and they confirmed that they were given the names of the alleged attackers. Now, in a whatsapp message from a local police spokesperson, it reads “a follow up investigation was done with no success, no arrests have been made and the police investigation is still underway.

VO 19 But, as the police investigation has continued, so have the attacks.

VO 20 Tony and Jean Robertson moved here from Cape Town six years ago.

UPSOUND Tony Robertson: It’s a totally different lifestyle from Cape Town.

VO 21 They planned to retire, but instead built two creches in the area.

UPSOUND Tony Robertson: It’s very fulfilling. We’ve got no children of our own, but children come here every day. They come to do their homework. Or whatever, come to play.

VO 22 In April this year, Tony and Jean were violently attacked.

UPSOUND Tony Robertson: We had just finished eating and two guys jumped in and they tied us up, tied me up really really tight.

VO 23 The men eventually left in Tony’s car after stealing electronics and a small amount of cash.

VO 24 Their car had a tracker and was recovered three hours later - completely stripped. There’ve been no developments in their case since.

UPSOUND Tony Robertson: They never came and took fingerprints. Police were a joke, really.

LINK: Locals believe the gunmen responsible for the wave of attacks are coming from outside the area. There’s a growing concern that this could have a devastating impact on tourism - the lifeblood of the local economy.

VO 25 So serious could the impact be that the mayor of the Mbashe Local Municipality, Samkelo Janda, drove two hours to speak to us.

UPSOUND Samkelo Janda / Mbashe Local Municipality Mayor: Government is not folding arms. One of the cries of the communities in this area , they would want to see a police station between the town and these towns along the coast. 12:23 A police station is under construction as we speak.

MASA: Are you confident they will be caught Mr Mayor?

UPSOUND Samkele Janda / Mbashe Local Municipality Mayor: I am. Yes it might take a little while because at the same time for their investigations they must ensure they are thorough in their investigations. We know collaboration becomes very critical to fight crime.

VO 26 But, community members feel police are failing them. Last week they protested outside the Elliotdale police station, 60 kms from Nqileni, to demand increased police visibility.

MASA: Did you ever want to pack up and leave the place?

UPSOUND Dave Martin: I can never lose my love and connection to this place and the community. I have to tell you right to live in this place in this hut with your wife, in the place, in the place where these criminals beat you, now there is this fear. I don’t want to go through that again. And I don’t want to see Rejane go through that again.

VO 27 Where once there was peace, now there’s anxiety.

UPSOUND Dave Martin: There’s a community here and these four guys are making them no longer feel safe here, and if we catch them it’s over right. It’s a problem with a very clear solution and that is to catch them.

VO 28 Rejane and Dave have been staying at the Bulungula Lodge since the attack.

NATSOUND Rejane: “But the tissue oil will heal the scar”.

VO 29 Their physical scars will heal…But the emotional damage won’t be undone until the police arrest those who brought violence to this remote and beautiful place.

Now, in a whatsapp message from a local police spokesperson, it reads “a follow up investigation was done with no success, no arrests have been made and the police investigation is still underway. VO 19 But, as the police investigation has continued, so have the attacks. VO 20 Tony and Jean Robertson moved here from Cape Town six years ago. UPSOUND Tony Robertson: It’s a totally different lifestyle from Cape Town. VO 21 They planned to retire, but instead built two creches in the area. UPSOUND Tony Robertson: It’s very fulfilling. We’ve got no children of our own, but children come here every day. They come to do their homework. Or whatever, come to play. VO 22 In April this year, Tony and Jean were violently attacked. UPSOUND Tony Robertson: We had just finished eating and two guys jumped in and they tied us up, tied me up really really tight. VO 23 The men eventually left in Tony’s car after stealing electronics and a small amount of cash. VO 24 Their car had a tracker and was recovered three hours later - completely stripped. There’ve been no developments in their case since. UPSOUND Tony Robertson: They never came and took fingerprints. Police were a joke, really. LINK: Locals believe the gunmen responsible for the wave of attacks are coming from outside the area. There’s a growing concern that this could have a devastating impact on tourism - the lifeblood of the local economy. VO 25 So serious could the impact be that the mayor of the Mbashe Local Municipality, Samkelo Janda, drove two hours to speak to us. UPSOUND Samkelo Janda / Mbashe Local Municipality Mayor: Government is not folding arms. One of the cries of the communities in this area , they would want to see a police station between the town and these towns along the coast. 12:23 A police station is under construction as we speak. MASA: Are you confident they will be caught Mr Mayor? UPSOUND Samkele Janda / Mbashe Local Municipality Mayor: I am. Yes it might take a little while because at the same time for their investigations they must ensure they are thorough in their investigations. We know collaboration becomes very critical to fight crime. VO 26 But, community members feel police are failing them. Last week they protested outside the Elliotdale police station, 60 kms from Nqileni, to demand increased police visibility. MASA: Did you ever want to pack up and leave the place? UPSOUND Dave Martin: I can never lose my love and connection to this place and the community. I have to tell you right to live in this place in this hut with your wife, in the place, in the place where these criminals beat you, now there is this fear. I don’t want to go through that again. And I don’t want to see Rejane go through that again. VO 27 Where once there was peace, now there’s anxiety. UPSOUND Dave Martin: There’s a community here and these four guys are making them no longer feel safe here, and if we catch them it’s over right. It’s a problem with a very clear solution and that is to catch them. VO 28 Rejane and Dave have been staying at the Bulungula Lodge since the attack. NATSOUND Rejane: “But the tissue oil will heal the scar”. VO 29 Their physical scars will heal…But the emotional damage won’t be undone until the police arrest those who brought violence to this remote and beautiful place.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The Eastern Cape's picturesque Wild Coast has been hit by a wave of violent crimes that is threatening its tourism market.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In the most recent attack, in August, Wild Coast community developers Dave Martin and his wife Rejane Woodroffe were violently attacked in their home, beaten up and kidnapped. They survived the ordeal, but say criminals from outside the area have been infiltrating the once peaceful villages, and communities are now living in fear of who will be next.
metadata.Summary: Dave Martin and his wife Rejane Woodroffe are founders of the Bulungula Incubator NGO and Bulungula Lodge and have lived in the area for twenty years. They were pistol-whipped and beaten with beer bottles during the August attack at Nqileni village in Xhorha Mouth. They were also kidnapped - the four gun-wielding attackers took them in their vehicle, but later released them and fled on foot. In April, a family that runs a creche in the area was also violently attacked. In February, Bulungula Education programme manager Lindiwe Tukane was attacked by two gunmen who stole her car and laptop.
metadata.Further information: The wave of violent incidents started in November, less than a year ago, with the murder of a trading store owner Peter Venter. He was killed in what's believed to have been a botched armed robbery. Community members believe criminals see the remote rural villages as easy targets. The closest police station to the Bulungula Lodge is two hours away. Dave Martin and his wife Rejane are committed to continuing their upliftment work. They have created 180 permanent jobs, and remain dedicated to addressing "systemic injustices that contribute to criminal behaviour".
